extracted.intended_audience: physicians, surgeons, and medical researchers studying urinary calculi and pathological chemistry
extracted.subtask_description: Laboratory and epidemiological examination of human urinary calculi: dividing specimens, chemically characterizing their deposits, tabulating occurrences, and relating case frequencies to population and local conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended hospital registry for statistical inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: A more extended system of registry in public hospitals is subservient to important statistical inquiries and conducive to pathological improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public hospitals might be made to important statistical inquiries by a more extended system of registry than is usually adopted, either in the metropolis or the country; such registers should enable relating numbers operated on to known populations. The author refrained from burdening other hospitals with inquiries where registers might not furnish the means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report case frequency relative to population (cases per annum / per capita)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present calculous case occurrence as cases per annum and as a ratio to population (e.g., 1 in 41,000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tabular summaries that show population, number of stone cases, cases per annum, and comparative frequency. Compare town vs country districts and compute per-capita rates to reveal relative predisposition (e.g., Norwich vs surrounding counties, Bristol city vs country district).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer analysis of divided specimens to surface-only examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses confined to the outer surface are insufficient; calculi should be divided to examine their interior structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only calculi that have been divided (or broken in extraction) admit satisfactory analysis of internal deposits. The author divided a portion (~330) of specimens to allow analysis and notes that many earlier examinations were surface-limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabulate sequential deposits from centre outward
rubrics_metrics.description: State, in tabular form, the consecutive deposits of different materials from the centre according to the most prominent character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting results, list deposits in order of their occurrence from the centre; indicate the principal material of each layer. Avoid treating mixed deposits as strictly unmixed — acknowledge blending and layered structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify calculi by deposit multiplicity and principal materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize calculi as consisting principally of one deposit, two deposits, three deposits, or four+ deposits, and name the constituent materials (e.g., lithic acid, lithate of ammonia, oxalate of lime, phosphate of lime, mixed phosphates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide counts for each class (the author gives counts such as Lithic acid: 81; Lithate of ammonia: 20; Oxalate of lime: 20; etc.). Note that many calculi are mixed and alternate in layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and report admixture in deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that no one deposit is strictly and unequivocally unmixed; deposits are blended with others to varying degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore mixed calculi. The author omitted detailed mixed-calculi description because strict purity is rare, but explicitly notes the prevalence of blended materials and the modifying effect on character and appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use chemical reactions to distinguish lithic acid vs lithate of ammonia
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate lithic acid and lithate of ammonia by tests such as evolution of ammonia on addition of pure potash, color, lamination, and behavior with solvents and acids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lithate of ammonia: small, gray, laminated, elicits ammonia copiously with pure potash; immersion in pure ammonia converts yellow laminated lithic acid into light-coloured lithate of ammonia; lithate dissolves in pure potash and yields ammonia on adding potash. Test behavior with alcohol, distilled water, dilute acids, and potash to infer inherent ammonia vs accessory salts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate source of evolved ammonia experimentally
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether ammonia evolved from a calculus arises from decomposition of ammoniaco-magnesian phosphate or is inherent to the lithate substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose specimens to alcohol/distilled water to attempt removal of accessory salts; test residues with acetic acid and carbonate of ammonia to detect triple phosphate; add pure potash to dried deposits to observe ammonia evolution and solubility. The author found evolution persisted after solvent extraction, arguing against decomposition-of-phosphate explanation in his specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and report presence of muriate (chloride) of ammonia
rubrics_metrics.description: Muriate of ammonia is traceable in lithate calculi and can be present in minute quantities in other calculi types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect via crystallization and sublimation, evolution of ammonia with potash, deposition of triple phosphate with magnesia and phosphoric acid, and formation of 'luna cornea' with nitrate of silver. Note that water can remove muriate of ammonia along with some lithic acid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider age and clinical context in composition interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Take into account patient age and clinical circumstances when interpreting composition (e.g., lithate of ammonia often associated with young subjects but can occur at all ages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report age associations (e.g., small gray laminated lithate calculi generally from young subjects), but verify by chemical testing because adult examples also occur. Recognize possibility of concurrent formation (e.g., minute calculi of different types formed nearly simultaneously).

rubrics_metrics.name: Give primacy to lithic acid formation in etiological assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: When appreciating tendency to calculous disorders and prevention, attention must be particularly directed to circumstances under which lithic acid is formed or developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epidemiological and preventive strategies should focus on factors that promote formation of lithic acid nuclei, since many calculi have lithic acid nuclei and might not have formed otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report sample coverage and caveats about unexamined specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the number analysed vs total collection and state whether the unexamined remainder is likely to differ materially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author analysed ~330 of 649 specimens and noted willingness to analyse remainder if divided; he also stated it was unlikely that the proportions of types in the remainder would differ materially. Always disclose such caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphological descriptors for oxalate of lime identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify oxalate of lime calculi by morphology: 'mulberry' appearance, colour range from dark brown to milk white, generally tuberculated/nodular texture, and occasionally amber-coloured or transparent white flattened octahedral crystals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document macroscopic shape and texture; look for flattened octahedral crystals (as noted in multiple specimens) and compare to known examples from animals and human cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume regional dietary factors uniformly produce calculous disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe regional correlations (e.g., ill-fermented farinaceous food, cyder counties) with caution; local anomalies and collateral circumstances may modify food effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local hospital statistics and population comparisons rather than broad suppositions. Note anomalies (e.g., Herefordshire exemption, Chippenham exceptional frequency) and consider other modifying factors (laxative tendencies of coarser foods, scrofulous diathesis in towns).
